idiom_name: (T, ok) comma-ok assignment and (T, error) returns, with *T as the optional pointer
implementation_notes: Go has no option type; absence travels as an extra return value that every call site has to consume. The comma-ok form is defined by the language for map lookups, type assertions and channel receives - the official blog describes the two-value assignment i, ok := m["route"] where ok is a bool that reports whether the key existed - and the same shape carries failures as (T, error), the convention the whole standard library is built on. A nil pointer (*T) is Go's nullable reference, but it cannot be distinguished from a pointer to an invalid value and dereferencing it panics, so prefer the comma-ok form; for values that come from nullable storage the standard library's database/sql wrappers carry a Valid flag for exactly that reason. The classic hand-written Maybe is not idiomatic in Go.
pitfalls: The zero value is indistinguishable from an absent value: a map[string]int lookup returns 0 for a missing key, so a legitimate 0 needs the two-value form.
A nil map is readable but writing to it panics, and nil pointers prove nothing about the pointed-to value - nil is not a general absence marker.
Returning a pointer to a zero value to avoid the second return value is the classic misreading: callers then have to check both nil and zero.
The compiler does not force the check: for maps a single-value assignment is legal (type assertions are not), so a missed ok has to be caught by review or linters.
